w: What's tested What each female organ does, and the ovary's two jobs Where the egg stops in meiosis, twice, and what restarts it The five follicle stages, how to spot each one, and the layers of the big follicle's wall FSH grows the follicles; LH releases the egg Ovulation, the corpus luteum and the corpus albicans How the ovary's cycle and the uterus's cycle line up, and his hormone graph Functionalis versus basalis, their arteries, and why a period starts The lining of the tube, uterus, cervix and vagina The breast: prolactin makes milk, oxytocin lets it out The big picture These notes follow Dr. Herr's recording (posted Friday afternoon, 11/6) and his slides. The ovary makes eggs and hormones. The tube carries the egg. The uterus takes the embryo. The cervix opens into the vagina. The vagina receives the sperm. The breasts are extra organs that belong with the system. Periods start between 9 and 14 (menarche). They stop between 45 and 55 (menopause), when the ovaries stop making both eggs and hormones. A cycle is about 28 days: 28 to 30 on his slide, 28 to 33 in the recording. The ovary The outside part, the cortex, holds the follicles. The inside part, the medulla, is loose tissue full of vessels and nerves. The surface layer is called the germinal epithelium, but that's a bad name: it makes no eggs. The ovary makes two kinds of steroid. Estrogen makes the sex organs grow. Progesterone gets the lining ready for a pregnancy by making it secrete. Egg numbers 5th month of fetal life: about 5 to 7 million. The dividing stops here. Birth: about 1 to 2 million. First period: about 400,000. Each month: about 12 start growing, usually 1 is released, the rest die (atresia). A whole lifetime: only about 450 released. The two stops in meiosis This is the big one: starred on his slide and said twice. Stop 1: prophase of meiosis I. Every egg waiting in every follicle is stuck here, for years. Go: the LH surge finishes meiosis I just before ovulation. One big egg and one tiny polar body come out, because the cytoplasm splits unevenly. Stop 2: metaphase of meiosis II. This is the egg that gets released. Go: fertilization finishes meiosis II and makes the ovum and a second polar body. No sperm, no finish. The egg lives about 24 hours. Memory cue: "Pro before birth, Meta at release, Fertilize to finish." The five follicle stages Primordial: one layer of flat cells around a small egg (about 25 micrometers). Early primary: one layer of cube-shaped cells, now called granulosa cells. The egg is about 4 times bigger. The zona pellucida starts (you don't need its ZP1, 2, 3 names). Late primary: many layers of granulosa cells. The theca forms outside them. Secondary: fluid appears (liquor folliculi) and pools into one space, the antrum. The egg sits on a mound (cumulus oophorus) wrapped in one cell layer (corona radiata). Graafian: huge, about 20 millimeters, and it bulges from the ovary. This one ovulates. To name a stage, ask: flat or cube cells? One layer or many? Fluid or not? Bulging or not? It takes many months to go from primordial to Graafian, not one cycle: he stressed that. The big follicle's wall, from the fluid outward: granulosa layer, a thin basement membrane, theca interna, theca externa. He says you can pick them out on a slide. Granulosa cells talk through gap junctions but have no tight junctions, so there is no blood-follicle barrier. The testis does have one (Sertoli cells). Theca versus granulosa Theca interna: lots of blood vessels; answers to LH; makes androgens that become estrogen. Theca externa: fibrous tissue and smooth muscle. Granulosa cells: answer to FSH; make the follicle fluid and OMI, which keeps the egg waiting. FSH grows about 10 to 12 follicles; it takes LH (in the FSH plus LH surge) to mature and release the winner. He went back to show this twice. Ovulation The big follicle makes lots of estrogen, and that triggers the LH surge (the positive-feedback exception). LH makes the follicle wall swell with fluid and restarts meiosis. The fluid space swells until the follicle bursts through the ovary's capsule (tunica albuginea). The egg and its corona radiata land in the abdominal cavity near the tube's funnel (infundibulum), which catches them. LH turns the empty follicle into the corpus luteum. Corpus luteum Granulosa cells become granulosa-lutein cells: progesterone and estrogen. Theca interna cells become theca-lutein cells: progesterone. No pregnancy: it dies and fills with collagen from fibroblasts. That white scar is the corpus albicans. Pregnancy: a hormone from the placenta keeps it going. The cycle, side by side Days 1 to 5, menstrual: the functionalis is shed. Days 5 to 14, proliferative (also called follicular): follicles make estrogen; the basalis rebuilds the lining; glands are straight. Days 15 to 28, secretory (also called luteal): the corpus luteum makes progesterone; the lining is thick and its glands coil and secrete. His graph, by day: Follicles grow days 1 to about 10; ovulation days 13 to 15. Estrogen climbs from day 7 and peaks about day 12 or 13, then a smaller bump about day 23. FSH and LH peak together just before ovulation. (L16's slides say FSH stays down then; each lecture's questions go their own way.) Progesterone rises from day 14 and peaks about day 22. Why a period starts Progesterone drops, the spiral arteries clamp down, the functionalis runs out of oxygen and peels off the basalis. This was starred on his slide, and he went over it twice. Functionalis = the top layer, spiral arteries, comes and goes. Basalis = the deep layer with its own straight arteries, so it stays and regrows the top. The tube Four parts: infundibulum (funnel with fimbriae), ampulla (widest, where fertilization usually happens), isthmus (narrow), intramural (in the uterine wall). Lining: simple columnar with ciliated cells (beat toward the uterus) and peg cells (feed the egg). "I do want you to know some components of this." Its muscle layer is thin and poorly defined. It also makes the factors that get sperm ready (capacitation). The uterus Layers: endometrium inside, myometrium in the middle, perimetrium outside. Myometrium: longitudinal, circular, longitudinal. The middle circular layer has the big vessels (stratum vasculare). Estrogen controls how big and how many muscle cells there are. In pregnancy they get bigger and more numerous. (He left this slide for you to read.) The cervix Canal: mucus-making columnar cells in crypts. Watery mucus at ovulation lets sperm through. Thick mucus in pregnancy makes a plug: the cervix closes off. Where it pokes into the vagina it switches suddenly to stratified squamous: the transformation zone. The vagina No glands. The ovulation mucus is from the cervix. Stratified squamous lining, with lots of lymphocytes and neutrophils underneath, longitudinal smooth muscle, and an adventitia. The cells store glycogen; Lactobacillus turns it into lactic acid; the acid keeps germs down. Antibiotics that kill the lactobacilli remove that shield. The breast 15 to 20 lobes of tubuloalveolar glands, set in fat and collagen. When nursing, the duct ends branch and grow milk-making alveoli. Milk has lactose, caseins, fat, IgA, minerals and salts. Prolactin makes the milk. Oxytocin pushes it out. Cue: "Prolactin Produces, Oxytocin Outs it." Colostrum, the first 3 to 4 days, has more protein and IgA, not less.
